Not at all. I'm sorry, John. I don't seem to be providing much help. Well, would you say that?

No, that's fine. Because in my own mind, Rosie turned out to be a competent musician without individuality or without copying one person so that he can be classified in a school, or without developing an individuality which makes him the founder of a school.
My feeling is along the same lines, yes.

Both you and I, I believe, feel that the Chicago School, as far as clarinet was concerned, was based on the inventions or the conceptions or the styles of the school. The styles of Teschmacher and Pee-wee-Pee-wee, not distinctly a Chicagoan, historically speaking, but yet so compatible with the Chicago style. Well, first of all, is that assumption correct, that they might have founded the elements of the Chicago style, as far as clarinet?

It's my assumption, yes. The actual historical business is vague to me. I don't know exactly when or how often Pee-wee played in Chicago, but you can't discuss Chicago style without discussing Pee-wee's playing, I don't think.
Do you remember any others of their general category? The early first generation horn men?
Well, Rod Klass used to bum around with Tesch, and Bud Jacobson was in town, wasn't he? Bud is, to me, representative of Chicago style, beautifully.
And yet he, I think, would be one of the first to say that, well, he was trying to play the rules that Teschmacher laid down. He'd constantly refer to Teschmacher's solo as the right way to play it.
This is Klass or... Or Jacobson. Jacobson, really?
Yes.

Well, Jacobson told me once that he felt a little resentment of Teschmacher because he felt Teschmacher was a little overbearing in his playing. He kind of took over the band. He, I don't know, I don't know if he had particular volume, but he, but that crashing attack that he'd play with evidently riled some of the other members in the orchestras he was working with. They thought he was, he was fighting too hard, he was playing a little too desperately. But for my part, that's what I love. I, I only know the records, naturally. And that's what struck me, that, that cracking attack that he'd play with and, and other characteristics of, of good clarinet playing that we've been discussing in these other fellows. Uh, Tesch simply gave those, those, uh, considerations second place. If his intonation went sour or, or, or he squawked or something went wrong, so what? The, uh, that, that feeling, that he had to get the feeling in there.

Do you think it might have been, uh, just that he hadn't been playing long enough to command the instrument, that is five more years, and Teschmacher might have played with a clean execution, yet using the same, uh, uh, fierce dynamics? Maybe it's possible to play that way.
I strenuously doubt it. I, I don't think you can have everything. Maybe some genius will come along who can, uh,

Well, uh, Teschmacher seemed sometimes to be playing outside of the, uh, elastic limits of the instrument. And now, uh, my, my question was, I mean, might be, uh, rephrased. Would he, uh, realize the elastic limits and, and stay within them? And, or would he, uh, uh, explore the instrument till he found some other way to do, uh, uh,
Well, as, as he grew older, or would have grown older, he might have done that, but I would think that would be a function of growing older, rather than a function of his attitude toward playing.
Or be mellowing rather than, uh, uh, uh, actually performing.
He would have found that he had to continue to get work and, and to comply with the, uh,
As long as we're speculating, that's, uh, more likely.
Well, I, you know, I, I prefer to think that he wouldn't. I, I like him very much the way I hear him play. And his intonation doesn't bother me at all. He can play as flat as he likes for my books.
Well, I wondered if some of those things were, uh, also possibly a fault of his ear.
Maybe so.

Bud Jacobson developed his ear, so that that, to the point that that intonation was correct. And this, I think, he leaned on, uh, Teschmacher's lead, and said, uh, we can get an effect by playing flat, or, it doesn't matter if you play flat, but it was on the flat side. It wasn't on the sharp side. The bud would usually err.

I think that's true, and that's a problem that's been bothering me ever since I started to play. I'm afraid that, uh, myself, I have, uh, difficulties. I, I tend to play flat. Now, I don't know, uh, as you suggest, the, the, uh, causes, probable causes for this. It might be deficiency in ear. It might be simply that I was so affected by Teschmacher's and Jacobson's and Bud Freeman's playing, when I was awakening to music, that I, uh, adapted this flat feeling about, about playing. You know, Bud played quite flat in the early, early days playing tenor. But, uh, Freeman.
No, you know, uh, well, one other name before we go, uh, connect this back to New Orleans. Burkhoff.
Burkhoff can be easily mistaken for Teschmacher on this record. I think Sister Kate, and I forget the other side.
Well, then, in later years, he occasionally, uh, used the, uh, rough tone style. Oh, really?
Yeah. What?
Well, uh, he played with a hillbilly band, made a marvelous record.
Oh, I was wondering if maybe later on he heard Pee Wee.
Uh, called Gals Don't Mean a Thing. Did you ever hear the, that record? No, I haven't.
Well, that's a pleasure. I hope you, I hope you will.
It does, uh, surprisingly well in the, in the, oh, the Teschmacher Pee Wee style.

Well, that's interesting to me, and, and, it, it gives me the feeling that there were a great many clarinet players around that time. Let's, well, let's say 1930, to make a focal point. A lot of clarinet players around Chicago were playing generally in that style, and the style seems to have died about four or five years later, as suddenly as Prohibition died and so on. And I don't know why.
There was one New Yorker who did it reasonably well, Fudd Livingston.
Oh, yeah.
Now, how did Fudd get, figure in there? Did he get in touch with Pee Wee, or did he find it out by himself? Did he find it out by himself?
Did he find it out by himself? Well, now Fudd, now Fudd's alive, isn't he, living around Cincinnati area or something?
He found it in the family area, I believe.

Oh, did he? Yeah. Well, somebody told me that, that Fudd had recently told him that all he was doing was try to play like the other guys, namely Tesch and Pee Wee. Now, I think he did it awfully well.
Yeah. Fudd and Benny Goodman were together a little while in the Pollock Band. Do you think that there was a point of contact?

Yeah. Now, Goodman's something else. I don't know who influenced him. I don't mean to say it that way, but it's very difficult. John and I were talking earlier about who influenced Goodman and Lennon about Goodman's early playing. It was crackling hot and fleet and beautifully executed. But we can't, we can't decide where he got it from. I think, certainly on two separate occasions, on one, I think the record is After a While with Wingy Minow. I think it was on OK, reissued Columbia. Correct me if I'm wrong, he does a few trills that seem to me he'd simply gone next door from listening to Pee Wee play and try to do it himself. And then later on, with Clarinetitis and That's A Plenty with the trio, his playing is very much like Teschmacher. This was one, did I say, 31, I think it was made, Bob Consulman, Mel Stitzel.

Well, I wondered whether Benny might have been influenced by some of the colored fellows. He didn't speak about influences from Rapolo. Rapolo was with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings when Benny was learning the clarinet. And they might even have traveled on the lake boats together. Because the New Orleans Rhythm Kings frequently rowed as guests across the lake in bands that Benny was playing with.
Benny was about eight years old, I think. Benny was in the short bands, I guess.

But it was in the summer that Benny played his first lake jobs that New Orleans Rhythm Kings were around. As I remembered, Rapolo had left them by this time, so I guess we'd better drop Rapolo's name from a direct influence. But Rapolo had made the records that all the kids were listening to. The New Orleans Rhythm Kings were the most popular hot band in Chicago. And he would have that touch with it.
That's surprising to me because I can't find any Rapolo influence anywhere.
Not in Benny's playing with it. All right.
It might well be there, but I'm not...I can't find it.
One other would be Vali Defoe, who frequently plays Benny Goodman, Lake. They overlap every now and then in a conception. Twelve notes that might have been played by either one of them. Could be.

I know Vali's early work mainly from a record, I think 1924, under Spaniard's name. Why can't it be Poor Little Me and Everybody Loves My Baby? And... Gee, it's hard. I don't know where to place Vali. Vali, all I know is that I thought that was a wonderful record. Vali played beautifully. Now this is, of course, before Tesh, before Pee Wee. Where he got it from, who knows, John?

Well, I have a suggestion. Vali spoke of playing with Keppard. It probably was at Lorraine Gardens, and probably they allowed him to play the first set or two until Buster Bailey came over. He was playing on a theater job, I believe, and then played with Keppard later in the evening. But Vali was allowed to sit in until Vali came over. Now this sounds, if this is true, and was two or three years earlier, sounds as if both Buster Bailey and Vali might have been influenced by what was happening on the south side. They might have had the opportunity to hear Dodds, and a little later Noon and Bechet.

Well, that makes us suppose that Vali had no white influences at all at that time. He was listening strictly to the colored bands. And, of course, the great question under discussion is where did the distinctively hot style come from that we identify with the Chicago white clarinet players? It must be something innate. They were nervous or something? Who knows? They were desperate or anxious or something, and they got this particular quality into their playing that the colored players didn't have. Who knows? Perhaps because they played with more ease or more confidence, perhaps the white guys were very young and impressionable and over-anxious.
Well, they talked constantly of having made the tour of the south side, and do you think that it was an overall impression then, rather than a note-for-note imitative desire?

Bud Jacobson told me once that he knew Pee-wee in the late 20s, and that Pee-wee would listen to a record of Jimmy Noon's with his Apex Club Orchestra. I know that you know, which, of course, as everybody knows, has enormously fleet, low register work on it. And Pee-wee tried to imitate the choruses, every note. Now, in that connection, we know this much that Pee-wee deliberately tried to imitate Noon. All I can say is I'm very happy that he failed. I like Noon's work enormously, but I would much less rather have two Noons than I would have what we have Pee-wee Russell playing today.

Noon, in some respects, was superficial, and there was so much embroidery to his playing that sometimes either the melodic content or the hot content or the rhythm got lost in frills. Now, the frills generally were well-
He can be accused of that, I think.
They were not, but sometimes the embroidery was just too much.

I think so. Aesthetically speaking, yes, but it remains that Noon is a model for clarinet players, I think. His time was excellent. His tone was unique. He had a beautiful grace in his playing. Now, however fast...
You may also have shown how the change of register is...

Well, yes, that's very important. The quick moving between the registers, the staccato, octave and similar intervals. Yeah, and I hope that that influence isn't waning. Nobody much is doing it. And it should be done with restraint and discretion, of course.
Actually, you made two instruments out of it. It was a solo instrument in two ranges. Yeah. It's true. But speaking about...
We finish up on Noon, maybe. I don't think that he can be regarded as much of a progenitor of the hot Chicago style, because he didn't crackle.
Uh-huh.

He tried, but he played too easily for that. He had too much serenity about his playing. The younger white Chicago guys had something else in mind. They admired Noon's technique, and they learned all they could from it, and the bending of the notes and everything, but... Noon's influence stopped at the point of hot playing, and we were talking earlier, John, about Omer Simeon, and I was wondering if Omer Simeon wasn't a more important influence on the younger white Chicago players. I don't know.
You see a closer relationship, do you, between Simeon and the white style than between any of the other...

Somehow I do, and I don't know why, really. But he attacked, he seemed to attack the instrument in a different way than Noon, or Begard, or Darnell Howard, with... How can you put it? What adjectives can you use? He had ease. He knew what he was doing. He was... He didn't... He doesn't ever sound on the jelly roll, red hot pepper, sidesy. He does... He never sounds ill at ease, or nervous, and those are words I think you can use in connection with the Chicago style. But he tended that way. It's very hard to say.
He wasn't usually the soloist on early records, was he? The peppers you talk about might have been the first time that he appeared as a soloist.

For all I know. His ensemble work is excellent. Of course, there's another manner of approach to the style, the method of playing ensemble. Now, they tell me that Jelly wrote out all the parts of the red hot peppers. I don't believe it. It's impossible. But Simeon would move around in the ensembles in a way that kind of forecasts the hot style of playing.

Before we leave Noon entirely, I want to mention that several people were influenced into succeeding generations by Noon, according to their own testimony. Johnny Lane has spoken about Noon as being, in his mind, the model clarinet player. And if I remember correctly, Lane taught Joe Marsala.
Wow!
Marsala, in turn, made a record of... Could have been... I know that you know.
I believe he did, yes. Which is very close to Noon. I don't have it. I wish I did. Very close to Noon.
Very close to Noon.
So Marsala, as well, tried to emulate that.

So it might easily have extended through a couple of generations. Now, Marsala, in turn, has a new pupil, a fellow lately in town by the name of Bob Gordon, who is considerably respected. We'll watch and see if Noon, by any chance, gets all the way through to Gordon. That might happen.

Well, I certainly hope so. And I think there's a good chance of it, John. I know Gordon's playing, and I admire him enormously, although I resent and envy him. He's going to take my jobs away from me. He's 19. I think he's just turned 20. I don't know. He's going on the road with Muggsy Spanier next Monday, by the way. He adulates Marsala, and I think he has a great deal of the same lightness and deftness about his playing that Marsala showed. There's a sprightliness about Marsala's playing, never mind the tempo or the nature of the tune, that's quite unique. And as you say, it's going to be very interesting to watch this lineage as it expresses itself in Gordon's playing as the years go by.
Is there a... did you ever hear the band that Chet Roble had, which had the same instrumentation as Noon, that is an aldo clarinet and rhythm section? Boyce Brown was the aldo player.
Oh, wait a minute. A trio with Sammy Aaron on bass? No, no, no, no, this is six pieces.
Oh. Had Eli Phillips on clarinet.
No, I...

Well, this was a group that studied the Noon records to reproduce the Noon. And then, of course, they did a lot of other tunes, but they thought that if they started off with Apex Blues performed in the Noon manner, that they'd be able to build up. And by George, they were imitative to a very agreeable degree. So, Noon, with his orchestra as well as with his solo clarinet, lived on some... ... ...

Some of them on record, whether or not they have a continuing influence is a matter that's considerably problematic to you. You don't know whether they might or whether they actually do. Let's take some of the people in the first generation, and let's see if you remember specifically that they could have influenced some of the Chicago boys. Was Bechet to any extent imitated?
Not to my knowledge. Of course, the name Mesrose springs to mind immediately, and I think he probably worshipped Bechet. Still does.
Yet I wouldn't say in his playing there's a bravery.
I can't find any, no, that's right.
